stem: A 64-year-old man who smokes and drinks heavily has had progressive trouble swallowing solids and then liquids, with 8 kg weight loss. He has no history of heartburn or reflux. Endoscopy shows an ulcerated mass with a raised rim, and biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma.
oneliner: 64M + smoker and drinker + progressive dysphagia + weight loss + no reflux + ulcerated mass, squamous carcinoma → which part of the esophagus?
ask: Which part of the esophagus is most likely involved?

whyNot.B: A common site for **adenocarcinoma**; this tumor is **squamous** and he has **no reflux history**
whyNot.C: **Adenocarcinoma** arises here from **Barrett metaplasia**, which needs chronic reflux he lacks
whyNot.D: Tumors here are **gastric adenocarcinomas**, not **squamous** cell carcinoma
whyNot.E: This is where a **Zenker diverticulum** forms, giving regurgitation and halitosis; esophageal squamous cancer is commonest lower, in the middle third

why: **Squamous cell carcinoma** of the esophagus is driven by **smoking and alcohol** and arises in the **upper and middle** esophagus, most often the **middle third**. **Adenocarcinoma** instead arises in the **distal third** from **Barrett** metaplasia after chronic reflux.

idea.rule: Esophageal squamous = upper and middle, smoking and alcohol; adenocarcinoma = distal, Barrett.
also: Other squamous risks: hot liquids, achalasia, lye strictures, Plummer-Vinson
Squamous cancer is the commonest type worldwide
Adenocarcinoma is now the commonest type in the US, arising in Barrett mucosa

stem: A 34-year-old woman is stabbed from behind. The blade enters just below the middle of the left 12th rib and passes through the lower pole of the left kidney. CT shows its tip resting in the tissue directly in front of the kidney at that level.
oneliner: 34F + stab wound below left 12th rib + lower pole of left kidney injured + blade tip just in front of the kidney → ?
ask: Which structure lies directly in front of the injured part of the kidney?

whyNot.A: Lies in front of the **upper and middle** left kidney; this wound is at the **lower pole**
whyNot.B: Lies in front of the **upper** part of the kidney, above the level of this wound
whyNot.C: **Caps the upper pole** medially, far from a wound at the **lower pole**
whyNot.E: Touches the **upper lateral** part of the left kidney, well above a wound at the **lower pole**

why: The **splenic (left colic) flexure** and descending colon lie in front of the **lower pole** of the left kidney. The stomach, spleen and pancreatic body are in front of the upper and middle parts, and the suprarenal gland caps the upper pole.

idea.rule: Left kidney from top to bottom: suprarenal gland, stomach and spleen, pancreas, then colon.
also: Right kidney: liver, descending duodenum and hepatic flexure lie in front
Both kidneys lie on the diaphragm, psoas, quadratus lumborum and transversus abdominis
The right kidney sits slightly lower than the left because of the liver
The left suprarenal gland is crescent-shaped and sits on the upper pole and medial border

stem: A 22-year-old man notices a groin bulge when he strains. It runs down toward his scrotum along the spermatic cord, sits above the inguinal ligament, and goes back in when he lies down.
oneliner: 22M + groin bulge on straining, follows spermatic cord to scrotum, above inguinal ligament, reducible lying down → where does the sac lie?
ask: Where does the hernia sac leave the abdominal cavity?

options.A: Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, above the inguinal ligament
options.B: Below the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein
options.C: At the linea semilunaris, near the arcuate line
options.D: Through the umbilical ring in the midline
options.E: Lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, above the inguinal ligament

whyNot.A: That is a **direct hernia**, pushing straight through Hesselbach triangle; it rarely **follows the cord into the scrotum** as his does
whyNot.B: **Femoral hernia** lies **below** the ligament; his bulge sits **above** it
whyNot.C: **Spigelian hernia** bulges on the lateral abdominal wall, not in the groin **along the cord**
whyNot.D: **Umbilical hernia** is midline at the navel, not in the **groin**

answer: Lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, above the inguinal ligament (indirect inguinal hernia)
why: A bulge that **follows the spermatic cord into the scrotum** in a young man is an **indirect inguinal hernia**. The sac enters the **deep inguinal ring**, which lies **lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels**, and travels through a patent processus vaginalis.

idea.rule: Indirect hernias go through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; direct hernias push through the wall medial to them.
also: Direct hernias lie medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, in Hesselbach triangle
Femoral hernias lie below the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein
Indirect hernias are congenital, from a patent processus vaginalis
Indirect hernias are the commonest groin hernia in both sexes

stem: A 4-year-old boy has had months of watery diarrhea, bloating and loud bowel sounds after drinking milk. His symptoms stop when dairy is removed from his diet. He has not lost weight and has no blood in his stool.
oneliner: 4M + months of watery diarrhea, bloating, borborygmi after milk, stop on dairy-free diet + no weight loss or blood → where is the deficient enzyme?
ask: Where in the gut and the enterocyte is the deficient enzyme located?

options.A: Apical brush border of jejunal enterocytes
options.C: Lumen of the duodenum, secreted by pancreatic acini
options.E: Chief cells of the gastric body

whyNot.B: Lactose reaches the **colon** because it was not split; the colon has no role in digesting it, and the enzyme does not sit on the **basolateral** side
whyNot.C: **Pancreatic enzymes** (amylase, lipase, proteases) are secreted into the lumen; lactose is split by a **membrane-bound** enzyme, not a secreted one
whyNot.D: **Lysosomal enzymes** break down cell debris; a **dairy-triggered osmotic diarrhea** is a surface digestion defect
whyNot.E: **Chief cells** make pepsinogen; his **milk-triggered diarrhea** is not a gastric problem

answer: Brush border (apical surface) of small-bowel enterocytes, mainly jejunum
why: **Diarrhea and gas that follow milk and stop without dairy**, with normal growth and no blood, fit **lactase deficiency**. Lactase is a **brush-border enzyme** on the **apical** surface of jejunal enterocytes, so undigested lactose draws water into the lumen and is fermented by colonic bacteria.

idea.rule: Disaccharidases such as lactase sit on the apical brush border of small-bowel enterocytes, not in the lumen.
also: Sucrase-isomaltase and maltase are also brush-border enzymes
Pancreatic amylase works in the lumen, then brush-border enzymes finish the job
Brush-border damage in celiac disease can cause secondary lactase deficiency
Enteropeptidase also sits on the brush border, in the duodenum, where it activates trypsinogen

stem: In an experiment, volunteers eat a protein meal carrying a radioactive label, and the label is followed along the gut. Trypsin and chymotrypsin have already cut the protein into short peptides, and free amino acids later appear in portal blood.
oneliner: Labelled protein meal + trypsin and chymotrypsin made short peptides + free amino acids reach portal blood → where are dipeptides and tripeptides broken down?
ask: Where are dipeptides and tripeptides split into free amino acids?

whyNot.A: Trypsin and chymotrypsin act here and give the **short peptides** already described; the last split happens after uptake
whyNot.C: **Pepsin** in the stomach acts before **trypsin and chymotrypsin**, so it comes before the short peptides exist
whyNot.D: The colon lumen has **no peptidases** of its own, and the **free amino acids** have reached portal blood upstream
whyNot.E: The mouth acts before **trypsin and chymotrypsin**, and saliva has no protease

why: Luminal proteases make **oligopeptides**. The **final cleavage** of di- and tripeptides into amino acids is done by **peptidases in the brush border and enterocyte cytoplasm**. Amino acids then leave the cell into **portal blood**.

idea.rule: Luminal enzymes make small peptides; enterocyte peptidases finish them into amino acids.
also: Di- and tripeptides enter enterocytes through the PepT1 transporter
Free amino acids leave the basolateral side into portal blood
Enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border activates trypsinogen
Carbohydrates follow the same plan: amylase in the lumen, disaccharidases on the brush border

stem: A 62-year-old woman has a painful, bleeding mass at her anal verge, below the dentate line. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma.
oneliner: 62F + painful bleeding anal mass below the dentate line + squamous cell carcinoma → which node group is reached first?
ask: Which lymph node group does this tumor reach first?

whyNot.A: Drain the anal canal **above** the dentate line; her mass is **below** it
whyNot.B: Drain the **upper rectum**, not the anal verge
whyNot.C: Drain the gonads and kidneys and are reached late, not first, from a tumor **below the dentate line**
whyNot.E: Receive lymph from the **superficial** inguinal nodes, so they are the second station for skin-type anal canal **below the dentate line**

why: The anal canal **below the dentate line** is skin-type and drains to the **superficial inguinal nodes**, so a groin node is often the first sign of spread. **Above the line**, drainage goes to the **internal iliac nodes**.

idea.rule: Below the dentate line: superficial inguinal nodes. Above it: internal iliac nodes.
also: Below the line, venous blood drains through the inferior rectal vein to the systemic circulation
Above the line, the superior rectal vein drains to the portal system
External hemorrhoids (below the line) hurt; internal hemorrhoids (above it) are painless
Above the line, cancer is usually adenocarcinoma; below it, squamous cell carcinoma

stem: A 45-year-old woman has a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones. The surgeon dissects the triangle bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the edge of the liver, and clips the artery to the gallbladder there.
oneliner: 45F + laparoscopic cholecystectomy + artery clipped in the triangle bounded by cystic duct, common hepatic duct and liver → which artery gives it off?
ask: Which artery most commonly gives off the vessel that is clipped?

whyNot.A: Supplies the **left lobe**; the vessel in this triangle serves the **gallbladder** on the right side
whyNot.B: Passes behind the duodenum toward the pancreas, away from the **hepatocystic triangle**
whyNot.C: Runs along the lesser curvature of the **stomach**, not the gallbladder
whyNot.D: Gives rise to the **proper hepatic and gastroduodenal** arteries, not directly to a vessel in this triangle

why: The **cystic artery** usually arises from the **right hepatic artery** and runs in the **hepatocystic (Calot) triangle**, bounded by the **cystic duct, common hepatic duct and liver edge**. Surgeons clip it there before removing the gallbladder.

idea.rule: The cystic artery comes off the right hepatic artery and runs in Calot triangle.
also: Calot triangle also holds the cystic lymph node
The right hepatic artery itself often crosses Calot triangle and can be mistaken for the cystic artery
The cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct
A replaced right hepatic artery arises from the superior mesenteric artery

stem: A 26-year-old man is stabbed in the left upper quadrant. At laparotomy, a laceration of the gastric fundus bleeds from the short gastric arteries, which are ligated.
oneliner: 26M + stab wound left upper quadrant + fundus laceration bleeding from short gastric arteries → which artery gives them off?
ask: Which artery gives off the short gastric vessels?

whyNot.A: Arises from the **celiac trunk** and runs along the **lesser curvature**, not to the fundus
whyNot.B: Comes from the **gastroduodenal artery** to the lower **greater curvature**, away from the fundus
whyNot.C: Runs behind the **duodenum** and supplies the head of the pancreas, not the fundus
whyNot.E: Gives the gastroduodenal and proper hepatic arteries, which go to the **right-sided** structures

why: The **short gastric arteries** supply the **gastric fundus** and arise from the **splenic artery**. The splenic artery also gives the **left gastroepiploic artery** along the greater curvature.

idea.rule: The splenic artery supplies the fundus (short gastrics) and the left greater curvature (left gastroepiploic).
also: The right gastroepiploic artery comes from the gastroduodenal artery
The left gastric artery comes straight from the celiac trunk
The splenic artery runs along the upper border of the pancreas
The short gastric vessels run in the gastrosplenic ligament

stem: A 30-year-old man is taken to the operating room after a car crash with a deep laceration across both lobes of the liver. To slow the bleeding, the surgeon clamps the structure that carries the hepatic artery and the portal vein to the liver.
oneliner: 30M + car crash + deep laceration across both liver lobes + surgeon clamps the structure carrying hepatic artery and portal vein → which structure?
ask: Which structure is clamped to cut blood inflow to the liver?

whyNot.A: Part of the lesser omentum, but it holds the **gastric vessels** along the lesser curvature, not the artery and portal vein to the liver
whyNot.B: Holds the **ligamentum teres** remnant of the umbilical vein; it carries no inflow
whyNot.D: Carries the **short gastric vessels** to the spleen and stomach, not the liver
whyNot.E: Attaches the liver to the **diaphragm** and carries no inflow vessels

why: The **hepatoduodenal ligament**, the free edge of the lesser omentum, carries the **portal triad**: proper hepatic artery, portal vein and common bile duct. Clamping it (**Pringle maneuver**) stops hepatic inflow; **bleeding that goes on** then comes from the **hepatic veins or retrohepatic IVC**.

idea.rule: The hepatoduodenal ligament holds the portal triad, so clamping it controls inflow to the liver.
also: The epiploic foramen lies behind the hepatoduodenal ligament
The lesser omentum has a gastrohepatic and a hepatoduodenal part
The falciform ligament contains the ligamentum teres
Continued bleeding after a Pringle maneuver points to hepatic vein or caval injury

stem: A 19-year-old man has had worsening abdominal pain for 3 days and now also aches at the tip of his right shoulder. His temperature is 39 C, and his abdomen is rigid with guarding. An upright chest film shows a crescent of air beneath the diaphragm.
oneliner: 19M + 3 days abdominal pain + shoulder-tip pain + fever + board-like abdomen + free air under the diaphragm → which nerve carries the shoulder pain?
ask: Which nerve carries the referred shoulder pain?

whyNot.A: Carries **parasympathetic and visceral afferent** fibers from the gut, not sensation from the diaphragm, and it does not refer pain to the shoulder
whyNot.B: Carries **visceral pain** from foregut organs, felt in the epigastrium, not at the **shoulder tip**
whyNot.D: Supply the **outer rim of the diaphragm** and abdominal wall, so irritation is felt over the **lower chest and upper abdomen**
whyNot.E: Supplies the **shoulder joint and rotator muscles** from C5-C6, but has no fibers from the **central diaphragm** touched by the air and fluid

why: Fever, peritonitis and free air under the diaphragm mean a **perforated viscus**, and the irritated **central diaphragm** sends pain along the **phrenic nerve (C3-C5)**. The brain reads this input as coming from the **C4 skin over the shoulder tip**.

idea.rule: Irritation of the central diaphragm is felt at the shoulder tip because the phrenic nerve arises from C3-C5.
also: Subphrenic abscess or splenic rupture refers pain to the shoulder (Kehr sign)
Gallbladder inflammation touching the right diaphragm can cause right shoulder pain
Irritation of the outer diaphragm is felt in the lower chest or upper abdomen through intercostal nerves
Mnemonic: C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive

stem: A 55-year-old man has had progressive trouble swallowing and regurgitates undigested food eaten hours earlier. His breath is foul, and he hears gurgling in his neck when he swallows. A contrast swallow study shows a midline pouch behind the pharynx, arising between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus.
oneliner: 55M + dysphagia + regurgitates old food + halitosis + neck gurgling + pouch between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus → nerve to these muscles?
ask: Which nerve supplies the muscles bordering the pouch?

options.B: Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion
options.D: Parasympathetic fibers of the vagus nerve
options.E: Branchial motor fibers of the vagus nerve

whyNot.A: Supplies the **muscles of the tongue**, not the pharyngeal constrictors
whyNot.B: Sympathetic fibers go to **vessels and glands**, with no motor supply to skeletal pharyngeal muscle
whyNot.C: Supplies only the **stylopharyngeus** among pharyngeal muscles, not the constrictors bordering this pouch
whyNot.D: Parasympathetic fibers go to **glands and smooth muscle**, but these constrictors are **skeletal muscle**

answer: Motor (branchial) fibers of the vagus nerve via the pharyngeal plexus
why: A posterior midline pouch between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus (Killian triangle) is a **Zenker diverticulum**, a pulsion outpouching above a tight cricopharyngeus. Both muscles are parts of the **inferior pharyngeal constrictor**, which gets **motor fibers from the vagus nerve** through the pharyngeal plexus.

idea.rule: Pharyngeal constrictors are skeletal muscles supplied by vagal motor fibers through the pharyngeal plexus.
also: The stylopharyngeus is the one pharyngeal muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve
Zenker diverticulum is a false (pulsion) diverticulum that forms above the cricopharyngeus
The recurrent laryngeal nerve, a vagal branch, supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid
The cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

stem: A 32-year-old woman has had a painful swelling of her right cheek for a day, worse when she eats. A tender, firm area lies over the parotid gland, and a stone is suspected in its duct. The duct runs across the masseter and opens in the mouth opposite the upper second molar.
oneliner: 32F + painful cheek swelling worse with meals + tender parotid + stone in duct crossing masseter → duct passes through which muscle?
ask: Through which muscle does the duct pass to enter the mouth?

whyNot.A: The duct only **runs across the surface** of this muscle before turning inward
whyNot.C: Forms the **lip sphincter**, well in front of the molar where the duct opens
whyNot.D: Lies in the **temporal fossa**, far above and behind the duct
whyNot.E: Lifts the **corner of the mouth**; the duct does not pierce it

why: The **parotid (Stensen) duct** leaves the front of the gland, crosses the **masseter**, then **pierces the buccinator** to open opposite the **upper second molar**. A stone here causes pain and swelling that worsen with **meals** (sialolithiasis).

idea.rule: The parotid (Stensen) duct pierces the buccinator to open opposite the upper second molar.
also: The submandibular (Wharton) duct opens beside the lingual frenulum, and most salivary stones form there
Branches of the facial nerve cross the parotid gland but do not supply it
Parotid secretomotor fibers come from the glossopharyngeal nerve via the otic ganglion
The sublingual gland drains through many small ducts into the floor of the mouth

stem: A 68-year-old woman has had 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and a swollen abdomen. A firm, tender lump that cannot be pushed back lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. An abdominal film shows dilated loops of small bowel.
oneliner: 68F + colicky pain, vomiting, distension + tender irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle + dilated small bowel → which route?
ask: Which route did the hernia take out of the abdomen?

options.A: Lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, via the deep ring
options.B: Through the femoral ring, below the inguinal ligament
options.C: Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, in Hesselbach triangle
options.D: Lateral abdominal wall at the linea semilunaris
options.E: Pelvic floor through the obturator canal

whyNot.A: **Indirect inguinal hernia**: the lump lies **above and medial** to the pubic tubercle, not below and lateral
whyNot.C: **Direct inguinal hernia**: also **above the inguinal ligament**, mostly in older men and rarely strangulating
whyNot.D: **Spigelian hernia** in the lateral abdominal wall, nowhere near the **pubic tubercle**
whyNot.E: **Obturator hernia** appears deep in the pelvis with medial thigh pain, not as a visible lump in the groin

answer: Femoral canal, below the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vein
why: A lump **below and lateral to the pubic tubercle** in an older woman is a **femoral hernia**. The sac passes through the **femoral ring** into the femoral canal, under the inguinal ligament, and the narrow ring makes it the groin hernia most likely to **strangulate** and obstruct the bowel.

idea.rule: A femoral hernia passes below the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral vein, and strangulates easily.
also: The femoral canal holds fat and lymphatics, lying medial to the femoral vein
Indirect hernias pass lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through the deep ring
Direct hernias pass medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through Hesselbach triangle
Women get femoral hernias more often than men, but inguinal hernias are still their most common groin hernia

stem: A 52-year-old man has a groin lump that has slowly enlarged over several months and is now painful. It is a direct inguinal hernia, and bowel pushes out through the superficial inguinal ring. It compresses the nerve that runs on the outer surface of the spermatic cord and leaves the canal through that ring.
oneliner: 52M + enlarging painful direct inguinal hernia + bulge through the superficial ring + nerve on the outer surface of the cord compressed → which function is lost?

options.A: Sensation from the dorsal surface of the penis
options.C: Sensation from the skin of the anterior scrotum
options.E: Motor supply to the cremaster muscle

whyNot.A: Carried by the **dorsal nerve of the penis (pudendal)**, which runs under the pubic arch, not on the spermatic cord
whyNot.B: Supplied by the **perineal branch of the pudendal nerve**, deep in the perineum, not at the **superficial ring**
whyNot.D: Carried by the **lateral femoral cutaneous nerve** near the anterior superior iliac spine, far lateral to the **superficial ring**
whyNot.E: The cremaster gets the **genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve**, which runs **inside** the cord coverings, not on the **outer surface** of the cord

answer: Sensation from the anterior scrotum (ilioinguinal nerve)
why: The nerve lying on the **outer surface of the spermatic cord** as it leaves the **superficial inguinal ring** is the **ilioinguinal nerve (L1)**. It carries sensation from the **anterior scrotum**, root of the penis and upper medial thigh, and it has no motor branch to the cremaster.

idea.rule: The ilioinguinal nerve runs on the spermatic cord through the superficial ring and supplies the anterior scrotal skin.
also: Groin hernia repair can injure the ilioinguinal nerve, causing numbness or pain over the anterior scrotum or labium majus and medial thigh
The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2) runs inside the cord and supplies the cremaster
The posterior scrotum is supplied by the pudendal nerve (posterior scrotal branches)
The ilioinguinal nerve enters the inguinal canal through its wall, not through the deep ring
